newsitem.title: USA: U.S. MUNI FOCUS -- prices sag, but new deals do well.
newsitem.headline: U.S. MUNI FOCUS -- prices sag, but new deals do well.

text.p: U.S. municipal bonds in late afternoon trade on Wednesday were quoted from flat to down one-quarter to three-eighths of a point, but new issues appeared to have gone smoothly, judging by repricings.
New York City, which sold $739 million of general obligations, said it lowered yields in several maturities and sliced the top yield in 2016 to 5.95 percent from six percent.

The city said strong demand and market conditions helped it capture another $10 million of savings than was planned in fiscal 1998, which starts July 1, for a total savings of $50 million. Priority orders added up to $542 million, while another $210 million of retail orders were placed. The refunding bonds drew a grand total of $1.6 billion of orders.

Still, noting that the shorter maturities, which made up the bulk of the deal, were not repriced, speculated that some of these bonds might find their way to the secondary market. "I think there will be some bonds on the Street," he said.
Nor was New York City, one of the biggest municipal issuers, the only one to sell its debt at higher prices than first anticipated.

Cleveland Stadium, which sold $139 million of Certificates of Participation, saw the debt repriced with lower yields in several maturities, and the top yield in 2027 was cut to 5.67 percent from 5.70 percent, according to A.G. Edwards & Sons.
But secondary market activity was listless at best.

"It was very frustrating (trying) to get anything done. Everybody wants top dollar," a trader said, noting that as bids rose one to three basis points at the long-end, offers remained around unchanged, loosening spreads.
"There's a lot of apathy unless you're participating in a new issue," he added. "This whole month has been pretty disappointing."

One day after the Federal Reserve opted to leave interest rates unchanged, U.S. Treasuries fell sharply as traders fretted that the narrower trade deficit, which showed stronger exports, would cause the already strong Gross Domestic Product to be revised up for the first quarter.
The U.S. trade gap slid 19.3 percent to $8.51 billion in March. This was well below forecasts for a $10.3 billion gap seen in a Reuters consensus poll of economists.
June municipal futures ended down 16 ticks at 116-6/32, while June Treasury bond futures slid 18 ticks to 109-9/32. The MOB spread stood at a strong plus 221 ticks.
In the secondary market, Dade County, Florida Water and Sewer System Revenues of 2016, which pay a 5-1/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.66 percent, NET, up three basis points.
And Minnesota Agricultural and Economic Development Board Revenues of 2026, which pay a 5-3/4 percent coupon, were bid at 5.81 percent, NET, down one basis point.
